meta.titre: Linear momentum: conservation, recoil and impulse

sections.contenu_markdown: A loaded timber truck on the road from Kumba to Mamfe is far harder to stop than a bicycle, even at the same speed. A goalkeeper at a village match pulls his hands back when he catches a fast ball, and a seat belt in a minibus stretches slightly in a crash. Mass and velocity together make up an important quantity, momentum. The GCE asks you to define it, to state its conservation, and to use it in collisions and recoil.

items: Mass is measured in kilograms and velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; velocity has a direction.
Newton's second law is $F = ma$ and acceleration is $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$.
Vector quantities have both size and direction, so signs show direction on a straight line.

sections.contenu_markdown:
**Linear momentum.** The momentum of a body is the product of its mass and its velocity:

$$p = mv$$

The unit is $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ (equal to $\mathrm{N\,s}$). Momentum is a vector, in the direction of the velocity. Choose one direction as positive and give motion the other way a negative sign.

**Principle of conservation of linear momentum.** When bodies act on one another with no external force on the system, the **total momentum before** a collision or explosion equals the **total momentum after**, in a given direction.

**Collisions.** For two bodies of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ with velocities $u_1$ and $u_2$ before the collision:

- If they stick together and move with a common velocity $v$: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = (m_1 + m_2)v$.
- If they move apart with velocities $v_1$ and $v_2$: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$.

**Explosions and recoil.** If the bodies start at rest, the total momentum before is zero, so the total after is zero: $m_1v_1 + m_2v_2 = 0$. The bodies move in opposite directions, and the lighter body gets the larger speed. Examples: a gun and a bullet; a boy jumping from a boat; a rocket.

**Impulse.** A force acting for a time changes the momentum. $\text{impulse} = Ft = mv - mu$. From Newton's second law, $F = \dfrac{mv - mu}{t}$, the force is the rate of change of momentum.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the two bodies move together after impact.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Total momentum before $= $ total mass $\times$ common velocity after. Total kinetic energy is not conserved, because some is changed to heat and sound, but total momentum is always conserved.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When bodies start together at rest and then separate, such as a gun and bullet.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Set $0 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$, so $v_2 = -\dfrac{m_1v_1}{m_2}$. The minus sign shows the opposite direction. A heavy gun recoils slowly, a light bullet flies fast.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why airbags, crumple zones or soft landings reduce injury.
variantes.contenu_markdown: For the same change of momentum, a longer stopping time $t$ gives a smaller force, because $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{t}$. Airbags, seat belts, padded gloves and bent knees on landing all increase the time of the stop.

sections.enonce_markdown: A boy of mass $50\ \mathrm{kg}$ stands in a stationary canoe of mass $150\ \mathrm{kg}$ on a calm river. He jumps horizontally off the front of the canoe with a speed of $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ relative to the ground. Ignore the resistance of the water. Find the velocity of the canoe.

etapes.action: Choose a positive direction and find the initial momentum.
etapes.justification: Both the boy and the canoe are at rest, so the total initial momentum is zero.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Take the boy's direction as positive. Total momentum before $= 0$.

etapes.action: Write the momentum of the boy after the jump.
etapes.justification: $p = mv$ with the boy's mass and speed.
No external horizontal force acts, so the total momentum after must also be zero.

etapes.action: Solve for the velocity of the canoe.
etapes.justification: Rearrange to find $v$ and read the sign.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The canoe moves backwards with a speed of $1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, in the opposite direction to the boy.

items.erreur_markdown: "A $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ trolley at $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ east and a $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ trolley at $3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ west have a total momentum of $12\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$."
items.pourquoi_faux: Momentum has direction. The two momenta are opposite, so they partly cancel.

items.erreur_markdown: "After the two wagons couple, I use $(m_1)v = $ total momentum, with the mass of only one wagon."
items.pourquoi_faux: After coupling the wagons move together, so the mass in $p = mv$ is the total mass.
items.correction_markdown: Use $(m_1 + m_2)v$ on the right-hand side.

items.erreur_markdown: "Kinetic energy is conserved in every collision, so I can use it to find the speed after they stick together."
items.pourquoi_faux: Some kinetic energy is changed into heat and sound when bodies stick. Only momentum is always conserved.
items.correction_markdown: Use conservation of momentum for the sticking collision.

items.erreur_markdown: "Momentum is $mass \times acceleration$ and is measured in newtons."
items.pourquoi_faux: Momentum is mass times velocity, in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. Mass times acceleration is a force.

items.erreur_markdown: "The gun and bullet have equal and opposite momenta, so they have equal speeds."
items.pourquoi_faux: The momenta are equal in size, but momentum is mass times velocity, so the lighter bullet has the much larger speed.
items.correction_markdown: $m_gv_g = m_bv_b$ gives a small recoil speed for the heavy gun.

items.enonce_markdown: Calculate the momentum of (a) a ball of mass $0.4\ \mathrm{kg}$ moving at $25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and (b) a car of mass $1\,500\ \mathrm{kg}$ moving at $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

A trolley of mass $6\ \mathrm{kg}$ moves at $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ along a straight track and catches up with a trolley of mass $4\ \mathrm{kg}$ moving in the same direction at $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The trolleys couple and move together. Find (a) the total momentum before the impact and (b) their common velocity.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Total momentum $= 6 \times 5 + 4 \times 2 = 30 + 8 = \mathbf{38\ kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

(b) $38 = (6 + 4)v$, so $v = \dfrac{38}{10} = \mathbf{3.8\ m\,s^{-1}}$ in the original direction.

items.enonce_markdown: A football of mass $0.4\ \mathrm{kg}$ arrives at a player at $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and is kicked straight back at $15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The contact lasts $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$. (a) Find the change of momentum. (b) Find the average force on the ball. (c) Explain why a goalkeeper who catches the ball and moves his hands back over a longer time feels a smaller force.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Take the kicked direction as positive, so the arrival velocity is $-20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Change $= m(v - u) = 0.4 \times (15 - (-20)) = 0.4 \times 35 = \mathbf{14\ kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

(b) $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{t} = \dfrac{14}{0.02} = \mathbf{700\ N}$ in the kicked direction.

(c) Stopping the same ball changes the same momentum. A longer time $t$ in $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{t}$ gives a smaller force on the hands.

items_markdown: Momentum $p = mv$ is a vector measured in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$; choose a positive direction and give opposite directions a minus sign.
Conservation of momentum: with no external force, total momentum before equals total momentum after.
Coupled bodies: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = (m_1 + m_2)v$; collisions that do not couple use $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$.
Recoil: starting from rest, the total momentum stays zero, so the bodies move in opposite directions and the lighter one is faster.
Impulse $= Ft = \Delta p$; a longer stopping time means a smaller force, which is the principle of airbags and seat belts.
